title: Chapter XVII

teacherSummary.text: The creature demands a female companion as wretched as himself, promising to withdraw to South America. Moved and afraid, Victor agrees.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XVII,” how does Shelley show the demand for a companion? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the theme you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XVII develops the idea of the demand for a companion. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of theme and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses theme in Chapter XVII to complicate the reader's understanding of the demand for a companion. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XVII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the demand for a companion responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XVII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the demand for a companion. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: Is the creature's request fair? What risks does Victor consider? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include insurmountable, concede, trifled, protectors, sickened. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “But that cannot be; the human senses are insurmountable barriers to our union.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: Incapable of being passed over, surmounted, or overcome.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Debates on whether humans have natural rights to companionship and happiness echo Enlightenment philosophy. Now, why does this chapter matter? This bargain is the hinge of the plot; Victor's later choice will decide everyone's fate. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Theme, Characterization, Conflict.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot theme, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.

segments.activity: One-sentence claim plus one quoted piece of evidence.
segments.script: To close: in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about the demand for a companion, and back it with one short quotation. Hand it to me on your way out.
